analysis.one_liner: Bans predatory mortgage practices like loan flipping, financed credit insurance, and steering borrowers to high-cost loans.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first committee referral and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003, without a single committee or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written tough anti-predatory-lending rules into federal law. It would ban lenders from charging prepayment penalties on home loans, financing credit insurance into mortgages, repeatedly refinancing a borrower into worse loans (called flipping), charging for services never provided, and steering borrowers who qualify for normal mortgages into high-cost ones. For the most expensive loans, it would require proof the borrower can repay and completion of homeownership counseling before the loan closes.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners and homebuyers, especially lower-income borrowers and seniors who are the main targets of predatory mortgage lending: they would keep more home equity instead of losing it to inflated fees, single-premium credit insurance, prepayment penalties, and serial refinancing.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits prepayment penalties on loans secured by a home, so borrowers can refinance or sell without paying a fee to escape a bad loan.
Bars lenders from financing credit life, disability, or unemployment insurance into a mortgage — a product long criticized for adding thousands in cost for little benefit.

Bans flipping — refinancing a borrower into a new home loan that has no reasonable, tangible net benefit — and prohibits steering consumers who qualify for conventional mortgages into high-cost loans.

Requires lenders making high-cost mortgages to reasonably believe the borrower can repay based on income and obligations, and to obtain certification that the borrower received HUD-certified homeownership counseling.

Prohibits fees for products or services never provided, direct payments to home improvement contractors without the consumer's countersignature, and creditor pressure on appraisers to inflate home values.

Prohibits required arbitration clauses in home-secured credit contracts and makes contracts with blank or missing terms void, and raises the civil penalty ceiling for Truth in Lending violations from $2,000 to $10,000.

analysis.who_pays: Subprime mortgage lenders and mortgage brokers who earned points, fees, yield-spread-style compensation, and prepayment penalties from flipping and steering; single-premium credit insurance sellers; and arbitration providers, all of whom would lose practices the bill outlawed.

drawbacks.text: Lenders argued that restrictions like an ability-to-repay requirement, a counseling prerequisite, and lowered high-cost thresholds can slow closings and reduce credit availability for borrowers with damaged credit, who would have fewer willing lenders.

The bill sets specific prescriptive rules (for example, capping late fees at 4% of the past-due payment and regulating fee timing in detail), which adds compliance costs across the mortgage market and gives regulators less flexibility than a general standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households targeted by predatory lending, the protections address practices that strip home equity and can end in foreclosure, and several provisions here later became standard federal law after the 2008 crisis. The costs — tighter credit for some risky borrowers and compliance burdens — are real but modest compared with the harm from flipping, financed insurance, and steering that the bill would stop. The bill is broad and prescriptive, so a fair reading is that some provisions could have used tuning, but its core protections aimed squarely at documented abuses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2001, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and sent to a subcommittee a month later — then sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action until Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on December 20, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
On January 14, 2002, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, the last recorded action on the bill.
The bill drew one cosponsor and never received a subcommittee or full committee vote, never reached the House floor, and died at the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subprime mortgage lenders and brokers were better off, because the practices the bill targeted — prepayment penalties, financed credit insurance, loan flipping, and steering borrowers to high-cost loans — remained legal, and the subprime lending boom continued growing until the 2008 mortgage collapse.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor record.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chair Rep. Michael Oxley (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee, and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so partisan positions were never recorded; the bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and it stalled in committee under Republican majority control.

industries.industry: Subprime mortgage lenders and mortgage brokers
industries.note: The bill outlaws core revenue streams of the subprime business: prepayment penalties, financed single-premium credit insurance, flipping fees on serial refinances, and broker compensation counted toward points-and-fees caps. Steering borrowers who qualify for cheaper loans into high-cost ones would also be banned.

industries.industry: Credit life and credit insurance sellers
industries.note: Financing credit life, disability, and unemployment insurance premiums into home-secured loans would be prohibited, eliminating a high-margin add-on sold largely at the lender's initiative.
Home-secured credit contracts could no longer require arbitration as the forum for disputes, shrinking the mandatory-arbitration business.

industries.industry: Home improvement contractors paid from loan proceeds
industries.note: Contractors could still be paid from home-loan proceeds, but only with the consumer's countersignature or via escrow, curbing fraud arrangements where lenders paid contractors directly for shoddy or never-performed work.
